articles.body_en: When I was an undergraduate, our professor showed us a short sci-fi film that scared me for years. The name of the film was *[Sight](https://www.shortoftheweek.com/2012/07/26/sight)*. It was about a man who woke up in his empty apartment. In the next scene, his augmented‑reality contact lenses come to life, changing the room completely. Now his room is fully decorated. We see recipes floating above the chopping board, news reports hovering at the periphery of his vision, and his lenses have turned his cooking into a game with points and achievements. The technology is everywhere, but invisible to the naked eye. It takes a dark turn when he goes on a date. He stares at the woman across from him through the lenses. Now, with the help of those lenses, he can see her and her information, but she has no idea. The prompts guide him, telling him what to say, how to sit, and what to order. It is truly terrible to lose the ability to make decisions on your own and allow the system to make them on your behalf so that you can “get what you want”. After the screening, I couldn’t sleep for nights. When I was growing up, I connected surveillance with the government watching you. Never in a million years did I think it could be built into someone’s eyes, secretly recording and dictating the conversation you share. Well, in *Sight*, the device and the man were one. I remember wondering whether this was a possibility. What if someone could walk into a room and scan every face for hidden data, without the other person ever knowing? The answer came sooner than I thought, and in the least exciting way possible. In 2024, [two Harvard students](https://www.nytimes.com/2024/10/24/technology/facial-recognition-glasses-privacy-harvard.html) walked through the Boston subway wearing Ray-Ban Meta smart glasses. Using PimEyes, a commercial facial recognition program, they found out who some of the strangers around them were. Their video went viral. Meta pointed out at the time that the glasses have a small white light, so people can see when they are being filmed. In early 2026, *[The New York Times](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/02/13/technology/meta-facial-recognition-smart-glasses.html)* [revealed](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/02/13/technology/meta-facial-recognition-smart-glasses.html) that Meta itself wanted to add facial recognition to the glasses, possibly as soon as 2026. Internally, the feature is called Name Tag. Through the AI assistant in the glasses, you would be able to recognise people and get information about them. Meta was still working out who would be recognisable. That could be people you are connected to through one of its apps, but possibly also strangers with a public Instagram account. It would not be able to look up everyone. Still, it comes uncomfortably close to the thing that had scared me about *Sight*. According to an internal document seen by the paper, Meta had been discussing the feature since early 2025 and identified “safety and privacy risks,” but the discussion then turned to the question of when to launch. The memo, from May 2025, was strikingly honest about the timing. “We will launch during a dynamic political environment where many civil society groups that we would expect to attack us would have their resources focused on other concerns,” it reads. So for Meta, the political turmoil in the United States presented an opportunity rather than an obstruction. There was no shortage of other concerns. ICE, for example, [uses facial recognition](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/01/30/technology/tech-ice-facial-recognition-palantir.html) on American streets. Democratic lawmakers [asked the agency to stop](https://www.markey.senate.gov/imo/media/doc/letter_to_ice_on_mobile_facial_recognition_tech1.pdf). “Face recognition technology on the streets of America poses a uniquely dire threat to the practical anonymity we all rely on,” Nathan Freed Wessler of the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) told the paper. Name Tag wasn’t the only plan. According to the paper, Meta was also working on glasses internally called “super sensing.” They would keep the cameras and sensors running all day and keep a record of your day, the way AI programs summarise a video meeting. Facial recognition would be a key feature, so the glasses could, for example, remind you of a task when you see a colleague. Mark Zuckerberg wondered whether the white light should then stay on, or whether there should be a different signal. In 2024, that light was still Meta’s answer to people’s concerns. Now the light itself is up for debate. In *Sight*, the woman across from the man had no idea. Meta wanted to launch Name Tag at a conference for blind and low-vision people first, and only then release it to everyone else. That never happened. For them, glasses like these could genuinely make a difference. The CEO of Be My Eyes, an app for people with visual impairments, spent a year talking to Meta about it. He told the paper how important and powerful it could be for this group of people. But in the memo, the conference is mostly a stepping stone to the wider public. That is how accessibility becomes a shield for a feature whose risks Meta itself knows. Meta already has a history with facial recognition. In 2021, Facebook [shut down the system](https://www.nytimes.com/2021/11/02/technology/facebook-facial-recognition.html) that let users tag friends in photos. The company paid \$2 billion to settle lawsuits in Illinois and Texas for collecting face data without consent. In March 2026, [three Democratic senators](https://www.markey.senate.gov/news/press-releases/markey-wyden-merkley-demand-transparency-from-meta-on-facial-recognition-technology-in-smart-glasses) asked Meta whether it would share biometric data from the glasses with the police and the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE. A month later, the ACLU and [75 other organisations](https://www.aclum.org/press-releases/aclu-and-75-organizations-sound-alarm-on-metas-plan-to-add-facial-recognition-technology-to-ray-ban-and-oakley-eyeglasses/) wrote an open letter to Zuckerberg. They cautioned that integrating facial recognition technology into consumer glasses would make it much easier to identify strangers at protests or outside clinics, and to link their names to data about their work, health and relationships. In these places, anonymity is extremely important to people seeking safety and protection. “Your glasses should not know my name,” said ACLU senior staff attorney Cody Venzke. A Meta spokesperson said the company was “still thinking through options” and would take “a thoughtful approach if and before” it rolled anything out. Meanwhile, the technology was already on millions of phones. In June 2026, [the tech magazine](https://www.wired.com/story/meta-smart-glasses-face-recognition-nametag-connections/) *[Wired](https://www.wired.com/story/meta-smart-glasses-face-recognition-nametag-connections/)* [revealed](https://www.wired.com/story/meta-smart-glasses-face-recognition-nametag-connections/) that since January, Meta had quietly been shipping parts of Name Tag in updates to the Meta AI app. The app has been downloaded more than 50 million times, and you need it for the glasses’ main features. Three AI programs were already on the phones. The first finds faces in an image, the second crops them out, and the third turns them into a faceprint, a unique digital code of someone’s face. The feature was not switched on yet. But according to *Wired*, the system was built so that once the feature is turned on, the app compares every face the glasses see with faceprints on the phone. Meta can add to that collection from its own servers. If the app recognises someone, the wearer gets a notification. All other faces are cropped and saved in a folder called “pending.” In a newer version of the app, the feature is called “Connections,” with the promise that you can “remember the people you met.” A researcher tested the system with a photo of the French philosopher Michel Foucault, who wrote about how surveillance keeps people in line. The app reported “Person recognized.” Meta “seems to have created the capacity to turn their customers into a distributed surveillance machine,” Cooper Quintin of the digital rights group EFF told *Wired*. Meta responded that “nothing has shipped to consumers” and that “no final decision has been made.” Shortly afterwards, the company [removed the code from the app](https://petapixel.com/2026/06/09/meta-removes-facial-recognition-code-from-ray-ban-smart-glasses-app/). In September 2026, parents and children from California and Illinois filed [a class action](https://www.pymnts.com/news/wearables/2026/meta-faces-lawsuit-over-smart-glasses-facial-recognition/) against Meta. They claim the company used their Facebook and Instagram photos without permission to develop Name Tag. Meta is not the only company making calculated decisions like this. Long before Meta’s glasses existed, other companies were already selling surveillance under the banner of safety. One of them is Flock Safety. Its automated licence-plate readers stand along roads and at the edges of parking lots in the United States. Towns brought them in to recover stolen vehicles and respond to crime. There was no national debate about whether small towns should join a larger, networked tracking system. Those networks are owned by a private company. Local police can search them, and through the police, so can ICE and the Border Patrol. Journalists and researchers figured out the full scale of it once they received Flock’s query logs. According to [a September 2025 investigation by the Virginia Center for Investigative Journalism](https://www.wvtf.org/2025-09-24/vcij-flock-surveillance-ice-immigration-enforcement), almost three thousand searches were made in a year on Flock’s network in Virginia. In those searches, police were using terms related to immigration, such as ‘ICE,’ ‘ERO,’ and ‘deportee.’ Roughly 9 out of 10 searches were made by police departments in other states. A spokesperson for the Virginia sheriff’s office that made the most searches confirmed that it did so when federal immigration authorities asked it to. People who believed they were paying for a camera that would catch car thieves are living on streets that have become part of a national deportation net. The University of Washington Center for Human Rights found at least eight local agencies in Washington state that appear to have enabled data-sharing with the US Border Patrol. In the report *[Leaving the Door Wide Open](https://jsis.washington.edu/humanrights/2025/10/21/leaving-the-door-wide-open/)*, published in October 2025, the researchers describe the set-up as effectively a “front door” to federal access. On paper, there is no mass-surveillance program, and no one is responsible for it. Flock will tell you that [it has no contract with ICE](https://www.flocksafety.com/blog/does-flock-share-data-with-ice). Local police say they respond only to lawful requests. And the Border Patrol is only using tools the town agreed to. Individually, each excuse makes sense, which is exactly why it’s so hard to fight. Amazon’s Ring uses the same kind of infrastructure. But it is being sold with a nicer, more homey story. This year’s Super Bowl ad shows a lost dog returning home safely with the help of the Ring “Search Party” feature. Using the neighborhood’s cameras, a trail of clips is woven, and at last, the dog appears at the right door. It presents networked surveillance as something warm and communal. Privacy advocates were quick to point out that the system built to track the dog could also easily track a person. Ring had also planned a partnership with Flock Safety that would permit police using Flock to request footage captured by Ring cameras. Amid the backlash to the ad, [Ring ended the partnership](https://abc7news.com/post/ring-flock-partnership-amazon-scraps-surveillance-company-safety-super-bowl-commercial-backlash/18596207/) before it even started. Ring emphasised that no customer footage had ever been sent to Flock. But countless cameras were still operating. Their footage is stored on company servers and can be searched later. Taken together, these systems show how technical infrastructure builds archives of ordinary lives. Companies often say they only keep data for a short time. Flock, for example, deletes licence-plate data [after a few days or weeks by default](https://www.flocksafety.com/blog/how-does-flock-handle-license-plate-data-deletion). But whatever the police save in that time, or whatever ends up online, can stick around for years. Imagine a march in 2024 that hardly raises an eyebrow at the time. Then, four years pass, and a new administration comes into power and either changes a law or decides that a given group of people is a problem. Now those “innocent”-looking images from the 2024 march suddenly get a second look. No one had to decide ahead of time whether the 2024 march was dangerous. All that needs to happen is for someone later to type a term into a search box and pull up the people and license plates. People often say, “Nothing to hide, nothing to fear.” This is only true if the rules never change. Sex between men was decriminalised in Trinidad and Tobago in 2018, but it was later [recriminalised by a higher court in 2025](https://globalvoices.org/2025/03/29/as-trinidad-tobagos-court-of-appeal-reverses-buggery-law-ruling-does-the-colonial-grip-persist/). Because it was allowed at first, men could be openly gay. They marched in the country’s first Pride parade and shared photos online. Those images are still there. Anyone who wants to can now see who is gay. Sex between men carries up to five years in prison again. Prosecutions are rare, but laws like this fuel discrimination, harassment, and violence. After the ruling, activist Jason Jones said the court had “[effectively put a target on the back of LGBTQIA+ people](https://www.thepinknews.com/2025/04/04/trinidad-and-tobago-recriminalises-homosexuality/).” In July 2026, [the Privy Council](https://www.guardian.co.tt/news/privy-council-reserves-judgment-in-jason-jones-lgbtqi-rights-appeal-6.2.2622850.8c59a45796) in London, Trinidad and Tobago’s highest court of appeal, heard his appeal. At the time of writing, it had not yet ruled. People who have learnt that visibility is dangerous rather than protective understand this best. [Amnesty International looked at 21 European countries](https://www.amnesty.org/en/documents/eur01/8199/2024/en/) and found that freedom of expression and the right to protest are under threat. It discovered that surveillance of protesters creates fear and deters people from attending demonstrations and meetings. [Dutch researchers spoke with activists from Extinction Rebellion](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/20539517241307892). Young activists in particular are now more hesitant to take the lead. Many activists post less on social media, or have stopped altogether. Researchers have labelled this a “chilling effect,” referring to the moment when a person hesitates to act at all just because they feel watched. The fear of being arrested is bad enough. Even worse is knowing that some company is storing data about you beyond any democratic control. You don’t know what it has kept or when it might come back to haunt you. The work of American sociologist Ruha Benjamin makes it clear that this danger did not start with smartphones. Surveillance has always been a technology of control. For years, people in surveillance studies have been saying that not everyone is affected by it in the same way. Newer tools mostly reinforce old technologies of control rather than replace them. In her book *Race After Technology*, Benjamin introduces the phrase “New Jim Code,” after the Jim Crow laws that enforced racial segregation in the American South. She uses it to describe technologies that may appear neutral or even progressive but take white people as the default and disadvantage people of colour. Instead of clear segregation, bias is now built into algorithms and scoring systems, determining who gets housing, who receives credit, and who is subject to policing or denied opportunities. In the Netherlands, this is not just theory either. In the childcare benefits scandal, the Dutch Tax Administration used nationality as an indicator in a system that automatically flagged applications for childcare benefits as high-risk. In 2020, [the Dutch Data Protection Authority called this](https://nos.nl/artikel/2340965-toezichthouder-werkwijze-belastingdienst-discriminerend-en-onrechtmatig) unlawful and discriminatory. Thousands of parents were wrongly treated as fraudsters, and some had to pay back tens of thousands of euros. In December 2020, a parliamentary committee spoke of “[unprecedented injustice](https://www.parlement.com/kabinetscrisis-2021-kinderopvangtoeslagaffaire),” and a month later the Rutte III cabinet resigned. [According to Statistics Netherlands (CBS)](https://www.cbs.nl/nl-nl/maatwerk/2022/48/actualisatie-uithuisplaatsingen-toeslagenaffaire-2015-t-m-juni-2022), more than two thousand children of affected parents were placed in out-of-home care between 2015 and mid-2022. CBS did not investigate whether the scandal was the cause. The figures for facial recognition errors are too high to be overlooked. According to [a 2019 test by the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST)](https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/ir/2019/NIST.IR.8280.pdf), several commercially sold systems were less accurate at identifying Black women and Asian people than white men. In the 2018 [Gender Shades](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v81/buolamwini18a.html) study, Joy Buolamwini and Timnit Gebru tested systems that had to determine the gender of a face. For women with darker skin, they got it wrong up to almost 35 per cent of the time; for men with lighter skin, less than 1 per cent of the time. A face read by the machine as white and male almost never creates any trouble. Too often, it quite simply does not work for women with darker skin. It is more likely to mix them up with someone else, and at times it just doesn’t see their face at all. What is particularly painful is that they are seen as a problem instead of human beings. This tendency even has a name: “coded exposure.” Benjamin uses it to describe how technology both fails to see Black people and watches them more closely. It’s easy to call it a glitch and fix it with a few Black engineers and better training data, but Benjamin warns against this very concept: treating bias as “an unfortunate glitch in the otherwise neutral development of technology.” It isn’t a bug. In Benjamin’s words, it is “a kind of signal of how the system operates.” The software doesn’t exist on its own. For example, PredPol was one of the most widely used predictive-policing systems in the US. It was based on a model originally built to forecast aftershocks following earthquakes. PredPol then filled map grids with tiny red boxes every day, based on old crime data. The crime data is mainly about the places the police went to. It took the police back to the same blocks. The more police there are, the more stops and arrests there will be, which are then seen as proof that the system is right. As Benjamin writes, software using this kind of data “will always be more likely to direct police to neighborhoods like the one I grew up in.” The whole premise is therefore ruled by bias in the data, and the machine repeats it faster and to a greater extent than any patrol work could. Simone Browne demonstrates the patterns of surveillance and control that Black people lived under. In *Dark Matters*, she studies the different tools that made it easier to control people under slavery and colonial rule. She writes about the floor plan of the slave ship Brookes, where every enslaved person was packed in and mapped out before the journey. Hot irons were pressed into their skin so they could be branded as the property of their owners. Runaway slave advertisements were further evidence, reducing people’s existence to short descriptions of their individual marks and scars. One of the regulations, called the lantern laws, compelled enslaved Black, mixed-race and Indigenous New Yorkers over the age of fourteen to carry a lantern with a lit candle after sunset, so that they would never have the chance to move through the city unseen. In 1784, an anonymous letter writer in a New York newspaper complained about the cruelty of these laws. A “white drunkard” could “disturb the street til midnight, with impunity,” the letter said, while “a poor black girl of fifteen” whose candle was blown out by the wind “is hurried to gaol, and next morning ignominiously scourged in public.” These were the laws and other practices that led to a world where people were never hidden from the state. Today, when the police direct a facial recognition camera at a crowd in the city, they are doing what they have done for as long as they have existed, except that they now have a new engine. Benjamin and Browne are both characterising a similar divide. Some people are meant to be traceable wherever they go. Others move through the same streets without leaving a trace. And when the system makes a mistake, the stakes aren’t hypothetical. A wrong match can mean [a wrongful arrest](https://www.clickondetroit.com/tech/2024/06/28/detroit-paying-300000-to-man-wrongly-accused-of-theft-making-changes-in-use-of-facial-technology/), a job denied without an explanation, or a stop that turns dangerous. It could even cost a life. This isn’t just about the error rate, but about the question of who gets watched in the first place. The systems are aimed at Black and Muslim communities, undocumented people, activists, sex workers, and queer and trans people in hostile political climates. They are the first people on whom surveillance is tested, and they are hit the hardest. Name Tag, Flock, and Ring ask: Who gets to stay unseen? There are still people who can move through a city without leaving a digital record. They can join a protest without having their car’s license plate recorded in a police database. They have no fear of a neighbor’s doorbell camera capturing them on their way to the hospital. They can relax at a bar without worrying that someone might scan their face. But some people are born on the other side of that divide. Surveillance is generally seen as an external imposition on people. What we often overlook is that we are the ones buying cameras and attaching them to our doors. When we wear glasses that watch all day long, we record everyone around us. Even the people the glasses don’t recognise end up in a folder called “pending.” Flock cameras on your street and Ring clips shared on neighbourhood apps help build an archive that might outlast today’s laws. The surveillance fight now goes beyond back-end systems and laws. It enters our habits. This change is not equal for all people. The individuals already watched minutely by the police or their neighbours are the most affected. This visibility has almost never been neutral for them. It makes them more likely to be stopped today, and their data will still be on file when the rules change. ## Sources ACLU of Massachusetts (2026, April 13). articles.excerpt_nl: Een onderzoek naar hoe de NFT-tentoonstelling Reloading zich verhoudt tot dekoloniale narratieven binnen blockchain-technologie. Ontmantelt of reproduceert deze technologie bestaande machtsstructuren?
articles.excerpt_en: Research into how the NFT exhibition Reloading engages with decolonial narratives within blockchain technology. Does this technology dismantle or reproduce existing power structures?
articles.body_nl:
*Een uittreksel uit mijn masterthesis aan de Universiteit van Amsterdam, New Media & Digital Culture, 2022.*

Sinds de doorbraak van non-fungible tokens — kortweg NFT's — in 2021 is er een verhaal in omloop dat klinkt als een belofte. De technologie zou digitale kunstenaars eindelijk de mogelijkheid geven om hun werk te verkopen zonder tussenkomst van galeries, veilinghuizen of de traditionele poortwachters van de kunstwereld.

Het klinkt utopisch. En precies daarom is het de moeite waard om er een stap dichterbij te kijken.

## De onderzoeksvraag

In mijn thesis stel ik de vraag: hoe verhoudt het NFT-project *Reloading* — een samenwerking tussen ART X Lagos en het NFT-platform SuperRare — zich tot dekoloniale narratieven die gekleurd worden door blockchain-imaginaries? Anders gezegd: wat doen Afrikaanse kunstenaars met deze technologie, en wat doet de technologie met hen?

## Wat blockchain wel en niet doet

Een van de meest taaie misverstanden over blockchain is dat het inherent decentraal zou zijn. Dat is afhankelijk van het soort blockchain. *Permissionless* blockchains zijn open voor iedereen. *Permissioned* blockchains hebben poortwachters, en het zijn juist die laatste die door overheden en grote bedrijven worden omarmd.

## Wat blijft hangen

Wat ik aan deze thesis heb overgehouden is geen conclusie maar een methode. De vraag is niet *"is deze technologie goed of slecht?"*. De vraag is: welke machtsverhoudingen lopen er op dit moment door deze technologie heen, wie heeft daar baat bij, en wie wordt erin gevangen?

---

[Lees de volledige thesis (PDF)](dania-awin-thesis-2022.pdf)
articles.body_en:
*An excerpt from my master's thesis at the University of Amsterdam, New Media & Digital Culture, 2022.*

Since the breakthrough of non-fungible tokens — NFTs for short — in 2021, a story has circulated that sounds like a promise. The technology would finally allow digital artists to sell their work without intermediaries — without galleries, auction houses, or the traditional gatekeepers of the art world.

It sounds utopian. Which is exactly why it's worth looking closer.

## The research question

In my thesis I ask: how does the NFT project *Reloading* — a collaboration between ART X Lagos and the NFT marketplace SuperRare — engage with decolonial narratives coloured by blockchain imaginaries? In other words: what are African artists doing with this technology, and what is the technology doing to them?

## What blockchain does and doesn't do

One of the stickiest misunderstandings about blockchain is that it is inherently decentralised. That depends on the kind of blockchain. *Permissionless* blockchains are open to everyone. *Permissioned* blockchains have gatekeepers — and it is precisely the latter that governments and large corporations have embraced.

## What stays with me

What I took from this thesis is not a conclusion but a method. The question is not *"is this technology good or bad?"*. The question is: which power relations are currently running through this technology, who benefits, and who is caught in it?

---

articles.excerpt_en: Progressive organisations write diversity into their mission statements. So why does it stop at words?
articles.body_nl: Als student was ik actief bij University of Colour, een antiracistisch collectief dat voortkwam uit de studentenprotesten van 2015 aan de Universiteit van Amsterdam. We wilden het curriculum dekoloniseren en werkten daarvoor samen met universiteiten, musea en andere organisaties. Zelf was ik wel huiverig om na mijn studie binnen zo’n instelling te gaan werken. Ik zag niet in hoe verandering van binnenuit kon komen, uit dezelfde structuren die het probleem hadden veroorzaakt. Jaren later ging ik toch aan de slag bij een grote organisatie die zichzelf progressief noemde, en ik herkende meteen waar ik bang voor was geweest. Mijn collega’s spraken vol vuur over mensenrechten en gelijkheid, maar de organisatie zelf was duidelijk gebouwd op de normen van witte, hoogopgeleide mensen. Ik kon niet meer wegkijken van de kloof tussen wat ze naar buiten uitdroeg en hoe het er binnen aan toeging. Veel organisaties die zich progressief noemen, hebben diversiteit, gelijkwaardigheid en inclusie (DEI) inmiddels opgenomen in hun missie en hun vacatureteksten. Op het eerste gezicht is bijna iedereen het erover eens dat inclusie belangrijk is. Maar als het erop aankomt wie er wordt aangenomen en wie er promotie maakt, zijn een stuk minder mensen bereid om echt iets te veranderen. En zelfs als mensen van kleur wel binnenkomen, blijft de vraag of hun oordeel ook serieus wordt genomen zodra ze aan tafel zitten. De Amerikaanse socioloog Patricia Hill Collins gebruikt hiervoor de term ‘epistemische autoriteit’. Simpel gezegd gaat het om de macht om te bepalen wiens kennis telt en wiens kennis wordt afgedaan als zomaar een mening. Er is een bepaald soort vergadering waarin je bijna van tevoren kunt zeggen hoe het gaat lopen. Iedereen vindt gelijkwaardigheid en eerlijke kansen belangrijk. Maar zodra iemand oppert dat dit gevolgen kan hebben voor wie er de leiding heeft, verandert er iets in de ruimte. Niemand zegt hardop nee. Mensen slaan hun armen over elkaar of gaan ineens stijf zitten, en de sfeer wordt zwaar en kil. Daarna wordt het gesprek trager en voorzichtiger. In een organisatie waar ik werkte, was er steeds weer een nieuw excuus om alles bij het oude te laten zodra het over raciale rechtvaardigheid en leiderschap ging. Voorstellen om racisme een centrale plek te geven in de strategie stuitten op zorgen over ‘onze huidige achterban kwijtraken’ of ‘supporters van ons vervreemden’. Suggesties om meer leiders van kleur te benoemen werden afgeschoten met bekende zinnetjes: ‘we kunnen geen geschikte kandidaten vinden’, ‘we hebben nu iemand nodig’. Op een gegeven moment werd er een extern DEI-bureau ingeschakeld. Het bureau schreef een rapport over roddels en onderlinge spanningen, maar ook over racisme en het gebrek aan leiders van kleur. De organisatie koos ervoor zich alleen op de roddels en de spanningen te richten. De structuren waardoor mensen van kleur zich niet gehoord voelden, bleven onaangeroerd. Het wees ook op een draaideureffect, waarbij mensen van kleur wel worden aangenomen, maar snel weer vertrekken. Uiteindelijk draaide alles om het ongemak van witte collega’s, en de mensen voor wie het traject bedoeld was, kwamen nog verder buitenspel te staan. Wat begon als een vraag over structurele verandering, werd een vraag over toon en over hoe je verandering bespreekbaar maakt zonder de mensen die het altijd al comfortabel hadden van slag te brengen. Inclusie bleef welkom, zolang er maar niets veranderde aan wat er al was. In haar boek *On Being Included* (2012) laat de Brits-Australische wetenschapper Sara Ahmed zien dat deze weerstand zelden een luid en duidelijk ‘nee’ is. Die weerstand zit ingebakken in de instelling zelf. De diversiteitsmedewerkers die Ahmed interviewde op universiteiten in Groot-Brittannië en Australië, beschreven hun werk vaak als ‘met je hoofd tegen de muur lopen’. Die muur bestaat uit gewoontes. Wat een instelling steeds weer doet zonder erbij na te denken, zorgt volgens Ahmed voor ‘een gevoel van gemak en vertrouwdheid’ bij de mensen die er al werken. Het wordt gewoon ‘zoals we het hier doen’. Diversiteitswerk gaat tegen die gewoontes in. Hoe langer je blijft vragen om verandering, hoe zichtbaarder de muur wordt. Ahmed vat het zo samen: ‘Waar gewoontes gedoe besparen, zorgt diversiteitswerk voor gedoe.’ Ahmed noemt de beloftes die instellingen doen over diversiteit non-performatives: ‘ze brengen niet teweeg wat ze benoemen’. Dat een instelling belooft werk te maken van diversiteit, verandert nog niets aan wat ze doet. De belofte wordt vooral onderdeel van het verhaal dat de instelling over zichzelf vertelt: het bewijs dat ze deugt. DEI ontbreekt niet, het wordt ingelijfd. De instelling kan de taal van kritiek overnemen zonder dat die kritiek iets uithaalt. Ahmed beschrijft dit als een paradox: diversiteit wordt overal gebruikt als ‘officieel taalgebruik’, terwijl de mensen die het diversiteitswerk doen merken dat diezelfde instellingen ‘weerstand bieden aan hun werk’. Zelfs het aannemen van een diversity officer kan daar een teken van zijn. Diversiteitsmedewerkers krijgen de opdracht om ‘diversiteit tot een doel te maken’. Dat alleen al laat zien dat diversiteit er nog niet vanzelf bij hoort. Een van hen zei tegen Ahmed: ‘Misschien ben je er gewoon, want als je er niet bent, kan de universiteit niet zeggen dat ze aan de wet voldoet.’ Zo’n benoeming komt in de plaats van echte steun. Dit verklaart voor een deel waarom DEI zo vaak blijft steken in communicatie en symboliek. Dat komt niet in de eerste plaats doordat de mensen binnen organisaties het niet menen. Instellingen draaien nu eenmaal op hun reputatie, en vooral ngo’s zijn afhankelijk van donateurs en het vertrouwen van het publiek. De zorgen over ‘supporters van ons vervreemden’ die ik eerder beschreef, kwamen daar ook uit voort. Zwijgen kan een organisatie duur komen te staan, net als iets verkeerds zeggen. Maar de juiste woorden kosten weinig, zolang het bij woorden blijft. Hier zie je het verschil tussen inclusie als etalage en inclusie als zeggenschap. Inclusie als etalage gaat over hoe een organisatie zich presenteert en welk ethisch imago ze opbouwt. Inclusie als zeggenschap gaat over macht: wie de beslissingen neemt en wie mag bepalen hoe een professional eruitziet. Veel instellingen betalen graag voor de etalage. Aan de zeggenschap tornen is een ander verhaal, want dan moet iemand macht of comfort inleveren. De ‘business case’ voor diversiteit maakt die tegenstrijdigheid vaak nog scherper. Dat is het idee dat inclusie niet alleen moreel juist is, maar ook goed is voor de winst. Adviesbureaus herhalen dat argument al ruim tien jaar. Het bekendst zijn de rapporten van McKinsey: [*Diversity Matters* (2015)](https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/people-and-organization/our-insights/why-diversity-matters), *Delivering Through Diversity* (2018) en *Diversity Wins* (2020). Ze wezen allemaal op een verband tussen diversiteit aan de top en financiële resultaten. Het eerste rapport verdeelde de onderzochte bedrijven in vier even grote groepen, naar hoe etnisch divers hun leiding was. De bedrijven in de meest diverse groep hadden 35 procent meer kans om financieel bij de beste helft van hun sector in hun land te horen. De rapporten laten zien dat diversiteit en winst vaak samengaan, maar niet dat meer diversiteit ook tot meer winst leidt. Toch gebruiken organisaties ze sindsdien als het bewijs dat inclusie loont. Kritische wetenschappers waarschuwden al vroeg dat dit argument wankel is. [In 2007 schreef de Britse onderzoeker Mike Noon](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0950017007082886) dat je gelijkheid kwetsbaar maakt door die aan winst te koppelen. Zodra de cijfers geen voordeel meer laten zien, wordt het voor organisaties ook makkelijker om het morele argument voor rechtvaardigheid te laten vallen. In januari 2025 bleek hoe snel dat kan gaan. Binnen één week draaiden Meta en [McDonald’s](https://www.pbs.org/newshour/economy/mcdonalds-joins-other-companies-in-rolling-back-diversity-goals) allebei hun diversiteitsbeleid terug. Meta schreef in een [interne memo](https://www.axios.com/2025/01/10/meta-dei-programs-employees-trump) dat ‘het juridische en beleidsmatige landschap’ rond diversiteit in de Verenigde Staten aan het veranderen was. Als diversiteit zowel moreel juist is als goed voor de winst, waarom blijven instellingen zich er dan tegen verzetten? Dat ligt zelden aan een gebrek aan cijfers. Het gaat om macht. Een organisatie als geheel kan winnen bij diversiteit. Maar de mensen die er de macht hebben, kunnen er ook iets bij verliezen. Nu bewegen ze zich moeiteloos in een vertrouwde cultuur en bepalen zij wat professioneel is, met zichzelf als maatstaf. Daarom slinken DEI-initiatieven zo vaak tot workshops en verplichte trainingen. Trainingen zijn niet nutteloos. Maar instellingen kiezen er graag voor, omdat een vraag over macht daarmee verandert in een vraag over persoonlijke houding. De organisatie waar ik werkte, deed hetzelfde toen ze uit het hele rapport alleen de roddels en de spanningen oppikte. De [sociologen Frank Dobbin en Alexandra Kalev](https://hbr.org/2016/07/why-diversity-programs-fail) analyseerden gegevens van ruim achthonderd Amerikaanse bedrijven over een periode van dertig jaar. Ze ontdekten dat de populairste diversiteitsprogramma’s zelden invloed hebben op wie er wordt aangenomen en wie er promotie maakt. Verplichte trainingen bleken zelfs averechts te werken. Vijf jaar nadat bedrijven ze voor managers verplicht hadden gemaakt, was het aandeel zwarte vrouwen in het management gemiddeld met 9 procent gedaald. Het zinnetje dat ik steeds weer hoorde, ‘we kunnen geen geschikte kandidaten vinden’, is een van de meest voorkomende vormen van deze weerstand. Het probleem is zelden een tekort aan mensen. De vraag is wie als leider wordt gezien. Leiderschap wordt doorgegeven via ongeschreven regels die neutraal lijken, bijvoorbeeld over hoe gezag hoort te klinken en wie het voordeel van de twijfel krijgt. Het meeste onderzoek dat ik tot nu toe heb aangehaald, komt uit Groot-Brittannië en de Verenigde Staten. Maar in Nederland is het patroon hetzelfde. Voor haar rapport [*Leiderschap in kleur*](https://www.universiteitleiden.nl/binaries/content/assets/algemeen/bb-scm/nieuws/2-leiderschap_in_kleur-judi_mesman-2024.pdf) (2024) interviewde de Leidse hoogleraar Judi Mesman veertig mensen van kleur die na mei 2020 waren benoemd in een leidinggevende functie bij de overheid of in de cultuur, het onderwijs of de zorg. In die maand werd George Floyd vermoord en daarna nam de aandacht voor etnische diversiteit in organisaties toe. Mesman koos bewust voor die datum, zodat de ervaringen laten zien hoe diversiteitsbeleid nu werkt. Bijna alle veertig vertelden dat ze zich op weg naar de top hadden aangepast aan wat Mesman ‘de Witte norm’ noemt. Een voorbeeld is taal. Volgens Mesman ging het om ‘keurig Nederlands spreken, niet met een accent praten, of dat nu een Surinaams accent is of een accent van buiten de Randstad’. Ze schat dat een onbekende die alleen de opnames van de interviews hoort, er ‘minder dan een handjevol’ zou herkennen als iemand van kleur. De deelnemers dachten vrijwel allemaal dat ze met een accent nooit op deze positie waren gekomen. Eenmaal aan de top beschreven ze een ‘dubbele belasting’. Ze moesten de organisatie leiden en tegelijk omgaan met hun ‘anders-zijn’, terwijl ze van bovenaf nogal eens weinig begrip en steun kregen. Dat kon eenzaam zijn. Nogal wat deelnemers kregen het idee dat hun organisatie alleen de motivatie kon opbrengen voor kleine, cosmetische ingrepen en een mooi divers ‘plaatje’, maar niet voor diepgaande cultuurveranderingen. ‘Ik vind dat het te vaak is: “we willen diversiteit, maar verder willen we in onze cultuur niks veranderen”’, zei een van hen. Ook Mesman verwijst naar het onderzoek van Dobbin en Kalev naar trainingen. Wie ‘de eerste en de enige’ is, betaalt daar ook een prijs voor. ‘Als ik te veel ga nadenken over mensen die denken dat ik dit alleen heb vanwege mijn kleur, dan vind ik dat wel heel moeilijk. Mensen denken dan ja, dat is weer zo eentje die is aangenomen voor de foto’, vertelde een andere deelnemer. Mesman is in haar aanbevelingen heel direct. ‘Problemen in een organisatie rond diversiteit en inclusie worden niet opgelost door één persoon van kleur in een leiderschapspositie.’ Zonder ‘mandaat en breed gedeelde verantwoordelijkheid’ wordt representatie nog een vorm van isolement. In 1979 werd de Amerikaanse dichter en activist Audre Lorde uitgenodigd om te spreken op een feministische conferentie aan New York University. Haar panel was het enige waarin zwarte feministen en lesbiennes vertegenwoordigd waren en dat benoemde ze in haar toespraak. ‘Want het gereedschap van de meester zal het huis van de meester nooit afbreken. Misschien kunnen we hem er tijdelijk mee verslaan op zijn eigen terrein, maar echte verandering zullen we er nooit mee bereiken’, zei ze daar. Ruim veertig jaar later beschrijven de leiders in Mesmans rapport hetzelfde. Organisaties veranderen nauwelijks, terwijl de taal van inclusie eromheen alleen maar groeit. Als student geloofde ik niet dat verandering van binnenuit kon komen. Hoe langer ik binnen instellingen werk, hoe meer ik ervan overtuigd raak dat ik gelijk had. Op dit moment volg ik een leiderschapsprogramma voor mensen van kleur, samen met negen anderen, de meesten vrouwen van kleur uit de culturele sector. Het zijn getalenteerde, slimme mensen. In onze gesprekken herken ik steeds mijn eigen ervaringen in die van hen. Ook zij draaien in hun organisaties op voor het diversiteitswerk, zonder dat ze ervoor betaald worden. Naar hen wordt ook niet geluisterd. In Mesmans onderzoek grapten deelnemers meer dan eens dat ze eigenlijk dubbel betaald zouden moeten worden. Zelfs met al dat dubbele werk verandert er zo weinig. ## Bronnen Ahmed, S. (2012). *On Being Included: Racism and Diversity in Institutional Life*. Duke University Press. Associated Press. articles.body_en: *This essay is part of an ongoing series of living research. It exists both on paper and in practice. I invite your reflections, questions, and disagreements, and hope it can be a space where dialogue continues beyond this page.* As a student, I was part of University of Colour, an anti-racist collective that grew out of the 2015 student protests at the University of Amsterdam and set out to decolonise the curriculum. We worked with universities, museums, and other organisations, but I was wary of working inside an institution myself after I graduated. I could not see how change could come from within the structures that had caused the problem in the first place. Years later, I joined a large organisation that called itself progressive and immediately recognised what I had been afraid of. My colleagues spoke passionately about human rights and equality, but it was clear that the organisation was built around white, highly educated norms. I could not unsee the gap between what the organisation was saying publicly and how it functioned internally. Many organisations that call themselves progressive now write diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) into their mission statements and their job ads. On the surface, almost everyone agrees that inclusion matters. Far fewer are willing to change who gets hired or promoted. And even when people of colour do come in, there is still the question of whose judgement is trusted once they are in the room. Patricia Hill Collins uses the term “epistemic authority” for this. Which in plain words means the power to decide whose knowledge counts and whose is treated as just opinion. There is a particular kind of meeting in which this dynamic plays out almost predictably. Everyone agrees that equity and fairness matter. But the moment someone suggests that this might change who is in charge, the energy in the room shifts. It is not that anyone says no. People just cross their arms or suddenly stiffen, and the air gets heavier and cooler. After that, the conversation slows down and gets more careful. In one organisation where I worked, every time racial justice and leadership came up, there was another excuse for why things had to stay as they were. Proposals to centre race in the strategy were met with worries about “losing our current base” or “alienating supporters”. Suggestions to appoint more leaders of colour were blocked with familiar phrases: “we can’t find the right candidates”, “we need someone now”. Eventually an external DEI bureau was brought in. Its report named gossip and interpersonal tensions, but also racism and the lack of leaders of colour. The organisation chose to focus on the gossip and the tensions. The structures that made people of colour feel unheard were left untouched. It also pointed to a revolving door effect, with people of colour being hired and then leaving again soon after. In the end, the discomfort of white colleagues became the main concern, and the people the process was meant to support were sidelined even further. What started as a question about structural change turned into a question about tone, and about how to talk about change without unsettling those most accustomed to being comfortable. Inclusion was still welcome, as long as it changed nothing that was already in place. In her book *On Being Included* (2012), Sara Ahmed shows that this resistance is rarely a loud, visible “no”. It is ingrained in the institution. The diversity practitioners she interviewed at universities in Britain and Australia often described their work as “banging your head against a brick wall,” that is, hitting something that will not move. That wall is made of habit. What an institution keeps doing unconsciously, in Ahmed’s words, “creates a sense of ease and familiarity” for those inside it. It simply becomes “how we do things here”. Diversity work goes against those habits, and the longer you keep asking for change, the more clearly the wall shows itself. As Ahmed puts it, “While habits save trouble, diversity work creates trouble”. Ahmed calls statements of commitment “non-performatives”: “they do not bring about the effects they name”. A commitment to diversity does not change what the institution does. It becomes part of how the institution describes itself, proof that it is good. DEI is not absent but absorbed. The institution can take up the language of critique without letting critique do its work. Ahmed describes this as a paradox: diversity is used everywhere as “an official language,” while the practitioners doing the work experience the same institutions “as resistant to their work”. Even the hiring of a diversity officer can be a sign of this. Practitioners are asked to “make diversity a goal”, which already shows that diversity is not yet part of how the institution works. One practitioner told Ahmed they were perhaps “just there”, appointed so the university could say it was complying with the law. The appointment took the place of real support. This helps explain why DEI so often ends up as a matter of communication and symbols. That is not mainly because the people inside organisations are cynical. Institutions run on their reputation, and NGOs in particular depend on donors and public trust. The worry about “alienating supporters” that I described earlier came from the same place. Silence is costly, and so is speaking incorrectly. But the right words cost little, as long as they stay words. This is the difference between inclusion as performance and inclusion as governance. Performance is about how an organisation presents itself and the ethical image it builds. Governance is about power: who makes the decisions, and who gets to define what a professional looks like. Many institutions are happy to pay for performance. Changing governance is another matter, because then someone has to give up power or comfort. The “business case” for diversity often makes this contradiction sharper. It is the notion that inclusion is not only right but also good for profit. Consultancy firms have made this argument again and again for a decade. McKinsey’s reports *[Diversity Matters](https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/people-and-organization/our-insights/why-diversity-matters)* [(2015)](https://www.mckinsey.com/capabilities/people-and-organization/our-insights/why-diversity-matters), *Delivering Through Diversity* (2018) and *Diversity Wins* (2020) pointed towards a link between diversity in leadership and financial results. Firms in the top quartile for ethnic diversity were 35% more likely to have financial returns above the median for their industry in their country, according to the first report. The reports show a correlation between diversity and profit, not proof that one causes the other. Yet they became the standard way organisations make the case for inclusion. Critical scholars warned early on that this argument is fragile. In [an article from 2007, Mike Noon](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/0950017007082886) argues that associating equality with profit makes it vulnerable: if the numbers stop showing a gain, the moral argument for justice becomes easier to drop. How quickly that can happen became clear in January 2025. Within a single week, Meta and [McDonald’s](https://www.pbs.org/newshour/economy/mcdonalds-joins-other-companies-in-rolling-back-diversity-goals) both rolled back their diversity policies. In an [internal memo](https://www.axios.com/2025/01/10/meta-dei-programs-employees-trump), Meta wrote that the “legal and policy landscape” around diversity in the United States was changing. If diversity is both right and good for business, why do institutions keep resisting it? The answer is rarely a lack of data. It lies in power. An organisation as a whole may gain from diversity, but the people who hold power inside it stand to lose something: the familiar culture they move through with ease, and the right to define professionalism in their own image. This is why DEI initiatives so often shrink into workshops and mandatory training modules. Training is not useless. But institutions like it because it turns a question of power into a question of individual attitudes. The organisation I worked for made the same move when it took only the gossip and tensions from the bureau’s report. [Frank Dobbin and Alexandra Kalev](https://hbr.org/2016/07/why-diversity-programs-fail) analysed three decades of data from more than 800 US firms and found that the most popular diversity programmes rarely change who gets hired or promoted. Mandatory training could even backfire: five years after companies made it compulsory for managers, the share of Black women in management had fallen by 9% on average. The sentence I kept hearing, “we can’t find the right candidates”, is one of the most common forms of this resistance. The problem is rarely a shortage of people. It is about who gets recognised as a leader. Leadership is passed on through unwritten rules that seem neutral, like what authority is supposed to sound like and who gets the benefit of the doubt. Most of the research I have cited so far comes from Britain and the United States, but the same pattern shows up in the Netherlands. For *[Leiderschap in kleur](https://www.universiteitleiden.nl/binaries/content/assets/algemeen/bb-scm/nieuws/2-leiderschap_in_kleur-judi_mesman-2024.pdf)* (2024), Judi Mesman interviewed 40 people of colour who had been appointed to leadership positions in Dutch government, culture, education and healthcare after May 2020. George Floyd was murdered that month, after which many organisations started paying more attention to ethnic diversity. Mesman chose that cut-off on purpose, so that the stories would show how diversity policy works today. Almost all 40 said they had adapted themselves to white norms as they climbed up the ladder. Language was one example: speaking proper Dutch, without an accent, whether a Surinamese accent or one from outside the Randstad. Mesman estimates that fewer than a handful of them would be recognised as a person of colour by a stranger listening to the interview recordings. Most were convinced they would never have got this far with an accent. Once at the top, they described a double burden: running the organisation while also dealing with being seen as different, often with little understanding or support from above. It could get quite lonely. Quite a few participants felt that their organisations could find the motivation for small cosmetic changes and a nice, diverse picture, but not for deeper changes to their culture. “I feel that too often it is, ‘we want diversity, but otherwise we don’t want to change anything in our culture’,” one of them said. Mesman also refers to Dobbin and Kalev’s research on training. Being “the first and the only” has a price too. “If I think too much about people who think I only have this because of my colour, I find that really hard. People think, yeah, there’s another one who was hired for the photo,” another participant said. Mesman is blunt in her recommendations. “Problems in an organisation around diversity and inclusion are not solved by one person of colour in a leadership position.” Without “a mandate and broadly shared responsibility”, representation becomes another form of isolation. In 1979, Audre Lorde was invited to speak at a feminist conference at New York University. Hers was the only panel where Black feminists and lesbians were represented, and she pointed that out in her talk. It was there that she said: “For the master’s tools will never dismantle the master’s house. They may allow us temporarily to beat him at his own game, but they will never enable us to bring about genuine change”. More than forty years later, the leaders in Mesman’s report describe the same thing. Organisations remain largely the same, even as the vocabulary of inclusion expands around them. As a student, I did not believe that change could come from within. The longer I work inside institutions, the surer I am that I was right. At the moment I am taking part in a leadership programme for people of colour, together with nine others, most of them women of colour in the cultural sector. They are talented, smart people. In our conversations, I keep recognising my own experiences in theirs. They, too, end up doing the diversity work in their organisations without being paid for it. They are not listened to either. Mesman’s participants joked more than once that they should really be paid double. Even with all that double work, so little changes. ## Sources Ahmed, S. *Deze essay is gepubliceerd in het Engels.*

---

This essay began, as many things in my life do, with a conversation with my best friend while I sat in a café. Neither of us have children, but we found ourselves talking about how we would want to raise them: what it might mean to teach a child that mistakes are survivable and that being held to account does not have to mean being cast out. As we talked, I thought about the times we had lost and found each other again and again after conflict.

Relationships have never been a neutral topic for me. I grew up in a house where love did not arrive alone. Danger sat at the same table, punishment was ordinary, and a child learnt early that safety could vanish without warning. In that world, being wrong did not mean "I made a mistake." It meant "I might not survive this."

For years, that training came with me into every relationship I touched. Before anyone else could punish me, I did it myself, convinced that if something went wrong it must be my fault, that something in me was rotten. In the same breath, I punished others when they hurt me. Someone who disappointed me became a villain in my mind. When conflict appeared, I disappeared. I cut contact and found it almost impossible to stay open. No one had ever shown me how to do that.

Healing did not begin as a noble wish to become a better person. It began as a survival project, a question of how to stay alive in myself and how to function at all. My story is only one version of this, yet it rests inside a larger pattern. Many of us brace ourselves as soon as accountability enters the room. The words arrive dressed as punishment. What begins as "you did something harmful" is heard as "you are harmful," and "this behaviour must change" turns into "your character is on trial." Under those conditions, even necessary confrontation can feel like annihilation. Therefore, defensiveness, denial, and self-justification are not mysterious responses. They belong to people who have been taught, again and again, that wrongdoing makes them unworthy of belonging.

She calls us toward a love ethic, toward an understanding of love as practice, woven from care, commitment, responsibility, respect, trust, and knowledge. Taking that seriously means accepting responsibility for how we show up with one another and letting love be measured by what we do rather than by what we claim to feel. Many of us have learnt to hear "we need to talk" as the start of rejection, humiliation, or control rather than a chance to deepen the relationship. We pull back in whatever way we can. In close relationships, people cut each other off rather than staying in contact long enough to work through what happened. In political life, harm is turned into a public drama that creates shame and headlines while very little actually changes. Online, the same habits are amplified. People are cast out with a few posts or comments, and the speed of reaction leaves almost no space for nuance, reflection, or repair. Even the way many adults speak to children passes on the same lesson: that making a mistake means you are the problem.

Studies of parent-child relationships suggest that shame and guilt do not work in the same ways. Harsh, punitive environments are linked to stronger and more damaging shame responses, while warmer and more supportive relationships make it easier for children to recognise wrongdoing without collapsing into worthlessness. Shame goes after the self. Guilt, when it is taken seriously in a caring relationship, can turn a child's attention toward impact and repair. Where shame freezes, hides, and attacks back, guilt held in a trusting relationship can open a doorway to empathy and connection. A child who is repeatedly addressed as if they are the problem does not learn to do better. They learn to be vigilant, avoidant, or highly skilled at defence. Raising children with integrity means holding a fierce line on behaviour while protecting, just as fiercely, their sense of being worthy of love and belonging. The face across the table may be fully grown, but the reaction comes from much earlier, from the part of a person that learnt love could be withdrawn at the first sign of failure. In that sense, much of the resistance to accountability is not resistance to truth but to humiliation, exile, or emotional collapse. The act of denying responsibility becomes a means of maintaining one's integrity when accountability has always been seen as an attack.

None of this should be seen as a justification for engaging in harmful behaviours. Still, the damage is significant. However, taking harm seriously also means asking how defensiveness was learnt and how it protects people from feeling the full weight of what they have done. Work in restorative justice is helpful here because it shifts the question. Instead of asking only who is guilty and how they should be punished, the focus turns to what happened, who was affected, and what repair is needed. In many circles, that practice is literal. People sit together in the same room and speak about impact, responsibility, and what needs to change so that the same harm does not repeat. The point is not to erase what happened, but to face it together and decide what repair is possible. This sort of accountability is not more lenient; rather, it simply is more demanding of each and every person in the room.

When harm is met with punishment, people often learn to act sorry without being genuinely touched. They grow quiet, say what they think is expected, play the part of remorse, and wait for the storm to pass. Nothing in the relationship has to change. Loving accountability asks for something harder. It stays with what happened and with its impact until both people can feel the weight of it. In that space, the person is always more than the harm, and the harm is acknowledged because the person matters. These truths are held together. You try to keep faith with the person while still saying, as clearly as you can, that what they did cannot continue.

The actual work starts now, developing through conversation and focused attention. The focus shifts toward understanding the impact of what has happened, while holding responsibility in a way that does not collapse into self-hatred or punishment. Change takes shape gradually, as patterns of interaction are reworked and something more intentional begins to guide the way you meet each other. What sustains it is a steadiness that neither hardens into judgement nor slips into neglect. Care becomes deliberate, shaped by boundaries that make continued connection possible. From within that clarity, the future is no longer assumed but slowly reimagined, carried by a language that can hold both truth and attachment at once.

Instead of reading someone's character, attention returns to what actually happened. The relationship becomes the starting point, making it possible to speak from care for what exists between you and a belief that something more honest can take shape. The tone changes as accusations like "you always" or "you are" begin to fall away. What replaces them is a more grounded way of speaking, one that stays close to experience, names impact, and makes room for change. Softer language does not dilute the truth; it removes some of the theatre of shame and opens space for accountability that can be lived rather than performed.

To hold each other in this way asks for vulnerability from the one who raises the issue. Calling someone in with love means acknowledging that it matters enough for silence to feel like abandonment. The discomfort of honesty is chosen over the false peace of keeping everything inside. There is care in that choice, and there is risk. Love, in this sense, is not simple reassurance but a willingness to enter conflict without letting it become a reason to end the relationship.

The person who is called in also has work to do. In a punitive culture, the first impulse is often to protect your sense of self at any cost, and that protection can quickly become another way of avoiding responsibility. A different kind of listening is needed. Accountability can be heard not as a verdict on who you are, but as information about what you did and what it did to someone else. You might notice your defensiveness while still recognising the other person's perspective, or acknowledge that harm was caused regardless of intent. At times, it means asking for space to think so that you can respond rather than react. These are not ways of proving innocence, but of staying in the conversation long enough for something other than reflex to emerge, allowing guilt to move toward reflection instead of collapsing into shame.

When it comes to accountability, a love-based practice has to work on both sides. The one who names harm is asked to resist the pull of punishment, including the lure of superiority and the desire to win. This requires stepping away from simple stories with clear villains and victims, and from the satisfaction of feeling justified within them. The task is to remain with what actually happened, without turning the other person into a symbol.

The one who is called in faces a different demand. It involves turning away from defensiveness, denial, and the impulse to retreat into self-victimisation, as well as letting go of the idea that good intentions cancel out harm. Staying present long enough to hear the impact can feel almost unbearable, yet it is part of the work. Both people are being asked to step outside the familiar logic of guilt and to trust, at least in part, that discomfort can move something rather than only wound it. This is difficult because punishment often presents itself as seriousness; what looks like moral clarity can feel like the only responsible response, especially when harm is still raw. This is less about scripting every argument and more about establishing, before anything erupts, that conflict is expected, that care does not depend on perfection, and that everyone involved intends to stay accountable when things become difficult.

At the same time, they come to understand that actions have consequences, and that repair is part of living with others rather than an occasional performance after a crisis. Being held to account then becomes one of the ordinary ways love appears, not a sign that love is being withdrawn.

On a larger scale, institutions face their own version of this challenge. Many swing between bureaucratic punishment and vague therapeutic language, either turning harm into a file or dissolving it into abstraction. A more consistent form of rigour would mean building cultures where feedback, consequence, and growth can exist together in public and predictable ways, so that people know what happens when harm is named. In such places, harm is neither treated as an individual flaw to be expelled nor as something to be smoothed over, but taken up as a shared responsibility that calls for attention, learning, and, as far as possible, repair.

No set of practices removes the pain. Even at its most careful and loving, accountability still grazes the ego and touches places we would rather leave in the dark. To be called in, or to call someone else in, means agreeing to meet ourselves where we would rather not look. That encounter hurts. The point is not to deny that hurt or dress it up as growth, but to separate it from punishment. Pain is not automatically a sign that we are being cast out or condemned. Sometimes it is the feeling of a relationship insisting on truth, refusing the comfort of denial or pretending. Sometimes it is the ache of knowing that something more honest is being asked of us, that a different way of being together has become nonnegotiable.

The hardest work does not end with our own reactions. It is also cultural. Many of us have been trained to believe that being confronted means we are no longer loved, and that confronting someone else means becoming cruel. Those lessons run deep. They keep people away from the conversations that might allow relationships to change instead of quietly decay. Yet both stories are false.

A more demanding truth is that accountability can be one of the most tender forms of regard. To hold someone to account with love is to say, in words or in actions, that this mattered, that you still matter, that what happened cannot be swept aside, and that there is still a path, if you are willing to walk it, toward something better than denial or disappearance. That path is rarely smooth. It asks for courage, patience, and a tolerance for ambiguity. The difficulty is not a sign that love has failed. It is often the clearest sign that love is being taken seriously.
